alignment.note: Greek opens with the simple coordinating conjunction Καὶ ('and'), while the Vulgate uses the postpositive adversative-continuative particle autem; the Peshitta fuses the conjunction into the temporal subordinator ܘܟܕ ('and when'), recasting the paratactic Greek genitive-absolute opening as an explicit subordinate temporal clause.

Greek expresses time with a genitive absolute (ὀψίας γενομένης, 'evening having come'); Latin renders this with the ablative absolute Vespere ... facto, a precise structural calque; Syriac dissolves the participial construction into a finite verbal clause ܗܘܐ ܪܡܫܐ ('it became evening') governed by the preceding ܘܟܕ.

Greek and Latin express 'the Twelve' with an article/substantive plus the cardinal numeral (τῶν δώδεκα / duodecim); the Peshitta employs the single inflected substantive ܬܪܥܣܪܬܗ bearing a 3ms possessive suffix ('his twelve'), making the disciples' relationship to Jesus explicit, an idiomatic Syriac compression.
